description: Test your knowledge of MI5.1-5 | Musculoskeletal, Skin & Soft-Tissue Infections.

cards.text: What is the defining feature of anaerobic bacteria and what tissue environment do they require?
cards.answer: Anaerobes lack catalase and/or superoxide dismutase, making them unable to tolerate oxygen. They thrive in devitalized, ischemic tissue with redox potential below –300 mV.

tip.tip: No catalase = no oxygen tolerance. Remember: dead tissue = anaerobe habitat.

cards.text: Which Clostridium species causes gas gangrene, and what is its morphology on Gram stain?
cards.answer: Clostridium perfringens — a large, Gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobic rod with a characteristic box-car appearance.

tip.tip: C. perfringens = box-car shape. Type A is most common in wound infections.

cards.text: What is the primary virulence factor of C. perfringens in gas gangrene and what does it do?
cards.answer: Alpha toxin (lecithinase, phospholipase C) — destroys cell membranes, lyses RBCs, and kills muscle cells. Causes rapid tissue destruction without inflammatory cell infiltration.

tip.tip: Alpha toxin = membrane destruction. Key: PMNs are killed before they can respond (no infiltration = diagnostic clue).

cards.text: What is the hallmark histological finding in gas gangrene tissue?
cards.answer: Absence of leukocyte infiltration — toxins kill PMNs before they can respond, creating muscle necrosis without inflammation.

tip.tip: No PMNs on Gram stain or histology = pathognomonic for gas gangrene. Toxins kill the immune cells.

cards.text: What is the mechanism of action of tetanospasmin (tetanus toxin)?
cards.answer: Tetanospasmin is a zinc-dependent metalloprotease that cleaves synaptobrevin (VAMP), blocking release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA and glycine) from anterior horn cells, causing spastic paralysis.

tip.tip: Blocks inhibition = uninhibited spasms. Toxin travels retrograde along motor neurons to the CNS.

cards.text: Name three characteristic clinical features of tetanus.
cards.answer: Trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus (fixed grin), opisthotonus (arching of back), and generalized tonic spasms triggered by stimuli. Respiratory failure may occur.

tip.tip: Tetanus = the 'terrible triad' of trismus + risus sardonicus + opisthotonus. Spasms are stimulus-triggered.

cards.text: How is gas gangrene diagnosed microbiologically?
cards.answer: Gram stain showing Gram-positive rods with no PMNs (key finding); culture on anaerobic blood agar with double-zone hemolysis; Nagler plate showing lecithinase activity (opaque zone inhibited by antitoxin).

tip.tip: Nagler plate = diagnostic gold standard. Antitoxin-inhibited zone confirms C. perfringens.

cards.text: What is the primary prevention strategy for tetanus in India, and when are boosters given?
cards.answer: Tetanus toxoid (TT) vaccination: 3 primary doses in childhood + booster every 10 years. Neonatal tetanus is prevented by maternal TT immunization during pregnancy.

tip.tip: Booster every 10 years. Maternal TT prevents neonatal tetanus via transplacental antibodies.
